baptism.sub: For the baptism of a child or an adult
baptism.verse: Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.
points: New birth
Baptism is not only a name-giving or a family custom. It is a new birth by water and the Spirit: original sin is washed away and the child becomes a child of God.
Into the Church
The baptised person becomes a member of the Body of Christ, the Church. The whole parish receives a new member today.
The white garment and the light

The white garment and the lighted candle are signs of a life to be kept pure and bright. In the Eastern Churches holy Myron (Chrismation) is given together with Baptism, sealing the gift of the Spirit.
Parents and godparents
The promises made today are kept at home: morning and night prayer, the sign of the cross, Sunday {Q}.
homily: Dear parents, godparents and friends, today we bring this child to the font. Jesus said to Nicodemus, “No one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.” What happens here is a birth: the child was born once to you; today the child is born to God.

In Baptism original sin is washed away, and this little one becomes a child of the Father, a brother or sister of Christ, and a temple of the Holy Spirit. The child also becomes a member of the Church. That is why we celebrate it in the church and not only at home: the whole parish receives a new member.

The white garment says: keep this life pure. The burning candle says: keep this light alive. But a candle cannot guard itself. Dear parents and godparents, the promises you make today must be kept in your home: in the first prayers you teach, in the sign of the cross you trace on this forehead, in the Sunday {Q} you never miss.
Let us thank God for this child, and let us all renew our own Baptism today. Each of us was once carried to the font like this. May we live as children of God. Amen.
baptism.prayer: Heavenly Father, you have given this child a new birth by water and the Spirit. Keep the white garment unstained and the light of faith burning, and bless the parents and godparents who will lead this child to you. Amen.

opts.a: Through the waters: the story of salvation
points: Water at the beginning
At creation the Spirit moved over the waters (Genesis 1:2). God begins again with water.
The Flood and the Red Sea
Noah's ark and Israel's crossing are pictures of Baptism: death to the old, a road to freedom (1 Peter 3:20–21; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2).
The Jordan
Jesus goes down into the river, the heavens open and the Father speaks (Mark 1:9–11). What happened to Him now happens to this child.
Water from His side
From the pierced side of Christ came blood and water (John 19:34): the Church is born from the Cross.
homily: Dear parents, godparents and friends, today a small amount of water will be poured, but it carries the whole history of God's love. The Bible begins with water: the Spirit of God moving over the deep, bringing order and life out of chaos. Every Baptism is a new creation.

Think of Noah. The world was drowning in its own violence, and God saved a family in the ark, carried through the waters into a new beginning. St Peter says plainly that this was a picture of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21). Think of Israel at the Red Sea: slaves went into the water and came out free, while Pharaoh's power stayed behind. Today this child passes through the water too, and what stays behind is the power of sin.

Then the Jordan. Jesus had no sin, yet He went down into the river, to stand with sinners and to make the water holy. The heavens opened, the Spirit came down, and the Father called Him His beloved Son (Mark 1:9–11). In a few minutes heaven opens over this child as well. The Father says the same word over this little one: you are my beloved.

And finally the Cross. When the soldier pierced the side of Jesus, blood and water flowed (John 19:34). The Fathers of the Church saw there the two great sacraments, Baptism and the Eucharist, flowing from the heart of Christ. This font is connected to that wound. The life given today is bought at a price.

So, parents and godparents, you are not only arranging a family function. You are bringing this child into the great story of salvation. Tell this story at home. Show the child the baptismal candle every year on this date. Bring the child to the {Q}, where the life begun today is fed. The waters are deep, and the love of God is deeper.

opts.a: Teaching homily: what Baptism does
points: Sin is washed away
Original sin and, for adults, all personal sin and all punishment due to sin are forgiven (CCC 1263).
A child of God
The baptised becomes an adopted son or daughter of the Father, a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265).
A member of the Church
Baptism makes us members of the Body of Christ and gives a share in the priesthood of all believers (CCC 1267–1268).
A seal that cannot be erased
Baptism marks the soul with an indelible spiritual seal; it is never repeated (CCC 1272).
homily: Dear friends, people sometimes ask why the Church baptises infants who cannot yet believe. The answer is the same reason parents feed a baby before it can ask for food. Life is a gift we receive before we understand it. The Church has baptised children from the earliest centuries, because grace does not wait for our cleverness (CCC 1250–1252).

What happens today? First, sin is washed away. This child has done nothing wrong, but every human being is born into a wounded humanity, without the friendship with God that Adam lost. Baptism restores that friendship. Original sin is forgiven, and the child receives sanctifying grace, the very life of God in the soul (CCC 1263, 1266).

Second, the child becomes a child of God. Not in a vague sense, as all creatures belong to God, but by adoption: a son or daughter of the Father, a brother or sister of Christ, a temple of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). St Paul says that we have been buried with Christ in Baptism so that we may walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4).

Third, the child becomes a member of the Church. From today this little one belongs to this parish family and to the whole Catholic Church throughout the world. The baptised share in the priesthood of Christ: one day this child will offer prayer and life to God, and will have a right and a duty to be taught the faith (CCC 1268–1269).

Fourth, Baptism leaves a seal that can never be erased (CCC 1272). Even if someone later wanders far away, the door home remains marked with the sign of Christ. That is why parents and godparents promise today to bring the child up in the faith. The sacrament is complete; the growth is your task. Teach the child to pray, bring the child to the {Q}, and let your own lives show what a baptised person looks like.

communion.sub: For the day children receive the Body and Blood of the Lord for the first time
communion.verse: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
points: Not a sign only
What the children receive today looks like bread, but it is truly the Body and Blood of Jesus, given for them.
The manna and the true bread
God fed Israel in the desert with manna; Jesus gives himself as the bread that gives eternal life.
A first, not a last
The danger is that First Communion becomes the last. Ask parents to bring the children every Sunday.
Prepared hearts
Confession, the fast before Communion, reverence and thanksgiving afterwards.
homily: Dear children, today is one of the most beautiful days of your life. For many weeks you have prepared, learnt your prayers and made your first Confession. Today Jesus himself comes to live in your heart.

When the priest gives you the Holy Communion, it will look like bread. But Jesus said, “I am the bread of life.” It is really Jesus: his Body and Blood, his whole self, with all his love. In the desert God gave the people manna; today he gives you his own Son.

When you receive Jesus, close your eyes and speak to him. Thank him. Tell him about your family, your friends, your fears. He is listening. And remember: this is your first Holy Communion, not your last! Jesus wants to meet you every Sunday.
Dear parents, the beautiful clothes and photographs will soon be put away. Please do not put away the {Q}. Bring your children every Sunday, and receive with them. Amen.
communion.prayer: Lord Jesus, bread of life, today these children receive you for the first time. Stay in their hearts, make them hungry for you every Sunday, and keep them always close to you. Amen.

opts.a: The Last Supper and Emmaus
points: The night He was betrayed
Jesus gave His Body and Blood on the very night of betrayal (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). His love is stronger than our failures.
Do this in memory of me
The {Q} is not a reminder only; it makes His sacrifice present.
Hearts burning on the road
At Emmaus the disciples knew Him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35).
Sent out
After meeting Him, the two disciples ran back to share the news. Communion sends us out.
homily: Dear children, today you will receive Jesus for the first time. Let us go back to the evening when He first gave this gift. It was the night before He died. Judas had already gone out to betray Him, and the disciples would soon run away. On that very night Jesus took bread and said: this is my Body. He took the cup and said: this is my Blood (1 Corinthians 11:23–26).

Why that night? Because Jesus wanted us to know that His love is stronger than our weakness. He did not wait for His friends to become perfect. He gave Himself to them as they were. You do not need to be perfect today either. You need to be ready, prepared by a good confession and a heart that says: Jesus, I want you.

Then think of two disciples walking to a village called Emmaus on Easter Sunday (Luke 24:13–35). They were sad. A stranger walked with them and explained the Scriptures. When they sat down to eat, He took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them, and suddenly they recognised Jesus. That is what happens at every {Q}: first He speaks to us in the readings, then He gives Himself in the bread that has become His Body.

The host you will receive looks like bread, but it is not bread any more. It is Jesus, truly, really, wholly present: His Body, Blood, soul and divinity. Receive Him with folded hands and a quiet heart. After Communion, do not hurry to talk to your friends. Talk to Jesus first. Tell Him thank you, tell Him your worries, and ask Him for the people you love.

The two disciples at Emmaus did not stay at the table. They ran back to Jerusalem to tell the others. Dear children, today is not your last Communion; it is your first. Come back every Sunday. And dear parents, bring them, and come with them. Let this day begin a lifetime of walking with Jesus.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the Real Presence
points: Truly, really, substantially
Christ is present whole and entire under each species (CCC 1374, 1377).
Transubstantiation
By the consecration the whole substance of bread and wine becomes the Body and Blood of Christ (CCC 1376).
How to prepare
State of grace, one-hour fast, reverence (CCC 1385–1387).
The fruits of Communion
Union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sins, strength against sin, unity of the Church, love for the poor (CCC 1391–1397).
homily: Dear children, parents and friends, today our children receive the most precious gift the Church has. It is good for all of us to remember what the Church teaches about it, because the way we receive Communion shows what we believe.

The Church teaches that in the Eucharist Jesus Christ is present truly, really and substantially: His Body and Blood, together with His soul and divinity (CCC 1374). This is not a symbol only, and not a nice feeling. At the consecration, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ spoken by the priest, the whole substance of the bread becomes His Body and the whole substance of the wine becomes His Blood. The Church calls this change transubstantiation (CCC 1376). What we see remains the same; what is there is completely different.

Jesus Himself said it in Capernaum: whoever eats His flesh and drinks His blood has eternal life (John 6:54). Many disciples left Him that day because the teaching was hard, and He did not call them back to explain that He only meant a symbol. He let them go. The apostles stayed because Peter said: to whom shall we go?

Because He is truly present, we prepare. We receive only when we are in a state of grace; if we are aware of serious sin, we go to confession first. We keep the one-hour fast. We dress and behave with respect, and we receive with faith, saying Amen: yes, this is Christ (CCC 1385–1387).

And what does Communion do? It unites us to Christ, wipes away venial sins, strengthens us against serious sin, makes us one family in the Church and opens our hearts to the poor (CCC 1391–1397). Dear children, you will receive this gift many times in your life. Never let it become ordinary. Every time, it is Jesus.

confirmation.sub: For the celebration of the sacrament of Confirmation
confirmation.verse: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
points: The seal of the Spirit
Confirmation completes the grace of Baptism. The bishop anoints with chrism: “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.”
The seven gifts
Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2).
Witnesses
Not a graduation from the Church, but a sending into the world as witnesses.
A practical gift
Name one place where each young person will need courage this year: school, friends, social media.
homily: Dear young people, today the Holy Spirit comes upon you in a new way. You were baptised as infants; others spoke for you. Today you say your own “yes”, and the Church seals you with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.

At Pentecost the frightened apostles became bold witnesses. The same Spirit gives you his seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. These are not ornaments; they are tools for life.

Confirmation is sometimes treated as the end of catechism, the day after which we need not come to church. It is exactly the opposite. Jesus says, “You will be my witnesses.” You are being sent: to your school, your friends, your phone, your future work.
Ask the Holy Spirit today for one gift you need most. And come back next Sunday to the {Q}, where the Spirit keeps strengthening you. Amen.
confirmation.prayer: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of these young people. Seal them with your gifts, make them brave witnesses of Christ, and keep them faithful all their lives. Amen.

opts.a: Pentecost: from fear to courage
points: Locked doors
Before Pentecost the disciples hid behind closed doors (John 20:19).
Wind and fire
The Spirit came as wind and tongues of fire and they spoke boldly (Acts 2:1–4).
Peter changed
The man who denied Jesus to a servant girl preached to thousands (Acts 2:14–41).
Your Pentecost
Confirmation is your personal Pentecost: the same Spirit, the same courage.
homily: Dear candidates, picture the apostles after the Resurrection. They knew that Jesus had risen, yet they sat behind locked doors, afraid (John 20:19). Knowing the truth is not the same as having the courage to live it.

Then came Pentecost. A sound like a strong wind filled the house, tongues as of fire rested on each of them, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:1–4). The doors opened. The same men who had been hiding went out into the streets of Jerusalem and spoke about Jesus to people from every nation.

Look at Peter. A few weeks earlier he had denied Jesus three times, frightened by a servant girl at a fire. Now he stood before a crowd and preached the risen Christ, and about three thousand were baptised that day (Acts 2:14–41). What changed? Not his intelligence, not his education. The Holy Spirit changed him.

Today is your Pentecost. The bishop will lay hands on you and anoint your forehead with sacred chrism, saying: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. It is the same Spirit who came upon the apostles. You may not hear wind or see fire, but the gift is real. The Spirit gives wisdom to choose well, courage to stand for what is right, and love that does not give up.

You will need that courage. At school, on your phone, among friends, there will be days when it is easier to hide your faith. On those days remember this morning. You are not alone and you are not weak: you are sealed. Pray every day: Come, Holy Spirit. And keep coming to the {Q}, where the Spirit keeps the fire burning.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the sacrament of Confirmation
points: Completes Baptism
Confirmation perfects baptismal grace and binds us more closely to the Church (CCC 1285).
The rite
Laying on of hands and anointing with chrism on the forehead, with the words: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1300).
The seven gifts
Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:1–3; CCC 1831).
A character for witness
Confirmation imprints an indelible mark and is received once (CCC 1304).
homily: Dear candidates, families and friends, today the Church celebrates one of the three sacraments of Christian initiation. Baptism gave you new life, the Eucharist feeds that life, and Confirmation completes and strengthens it (CCC 1285).

The Catechism explains that Confirmation roots us more deeply in our being children of God, unites us more firmly to Christ, increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit in us, binds us more perfectly to the Church and gives special strength to spread and defend the faith by word and action (CCC 1303).

The rite is simple and ancient. The apostles laid hands on the baptised so that they might receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17). The bishop, a successor of the apostles, does the same today, and anoints the forehead with chrism, oil mixed with balsam and consecrated on Holy Thursday. Chrism gives Christians their name: Christ means the Anointed One, and we share His anointing (CCC 1289, 1294).

Isaiah names the gifts that rest on the Messiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:1–3). These gifts are now yours. They are not trophies for a shelf; they are tools. Wisdom helps you see life as God sees it. Fortitude helps you do the right thing when it costs you. Fear of the Lord is not terror, but the deep respect that never wants to hurt the One we love.

Confirmation marks the soul with an indelible character; it is never repeated (CCC 1304). You are now fully equipped as witnesses of Christ. Choose a saint whose name you take and get to know his or her life. Keep in touch with your sponsor. Above all, use the gifts: pray daily, read the Gospel, come to the {Q} and to confession, and do not be ashamed of the name of Christ.

betrothal.sub: For the betrothal or engagement in church before marriage
betrothal.verse: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner.
points: A free consent
The heart of the betrothal is a free promise. No one may be forced; the Church asks, and each answers freely.
God's plan from the beginning
“It is not good that the man should be alone.” Marriage is God's idea before it is ours.
Love that is patient
1 Corinthians 13 describes love as a decision, not only a feeling.
The time of preparation
Prayer together, the marriage preparation course, a good Confession, honesty about finances and families, and chastity.
homily: Dear brother and sister, today you stand before God and his Church and declare your intention to marry. This is not yet the wedding, but it is a holy beginning. The Church asks you whether you come freely, and you answer for yourselves.

In the very first pages of the Bible God says: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner.” Your love is not an accident. It belongs to God's plan from the beginning.

The weeks before a wedding are often filled with halls, dresses, food and invitations. Do not let them steal the real preparation. Pray together. Take the marriage preparation course seriously. Speak honestly about your families, your money and your hopes. Make a good Confession before the wedding.
St Paul tells us that love is patient and kind, that it bears all things and hopes all things. Ask God for that love now, and you will carry it into your marriage. Amen.
betrothal.prayer: Lord God, you created man and woman for each other. Bless these two who have promised to marry; prepare their hearts by your grace, and lead them in purity and joy to the day of their wedding. Amen.

opts.a: Tobias and Sarah: a marriage that begins with prayer
points: A journey guided by God
Tobias did not know the way, but the angel Raphael walked with him (Tobit 5).
Prayer before anything else
On their wedding night Tobias and Sarah first stood up to pray (Tobit 8:4–8).
Not lust but truth
Tobias asked God to see that he took Sarah with a sincere heart (Tobit 8:7).
Bless your road
Let these months of preparation be a road walked with God.
homily: Dear N. and N., today you promise each other, before God and your families, that you intend to marry. It is a beautiful moment, and also a serious one. Let me tell you about another young couple whose story is in the Bible, Tobias and Sarah.

Tobias was sent on a long journey and did not know the road. A companion offered to guide him; only at the end did he learn that his companion was the angel Raphael, sent by God (Tobit 5; 12:15). You too are starting a journey whose road you do not fully know. You will not see angels, but God walks beside you. Ask Him every day to guide you.

Sarah had suffered great sorrow before she met Tobias. Her life was not simple. When they married, the first thing Tobias did was not to celebrate, but to say to Sarah: let us pray. They stood together and blessed God, and Tobias said that he was taking Sarah not out of lust but with sincerity, and asked that they might grow old together (Tobit 8:4–8).

This is a model for your time of preparation. Let your relationship be built on prayer and on truth. Pray together, even briefly. Speak honestly about your hopes, your fears, money, family, children and faith. Respect each other's body and honour the gift you will give each other in marriage. Chastity before marriage is not a cage; it is a training in self-giving love.

Families, you too have a part. Support them, do not overload them with demands, and pray for them. Dear N. and N., may the God of Tobias and Sarah walk with you until the day of your wedding and every day after it, and may you one day say, as they did, that you have grown old together in His love.

opts.a: Teaching homily: preparing for the sacrament
points: What betrothal is
A public promise to marry; not yet the sacrament, but a serious commitment (CCC 1632).
Freedom of consent
Marriage requires free consent, without fear or pressure (CCC 1625–1628).
Marriage preparation
Couples should be prepared by catechesis and example (CCC 1632).
Chastity in engagement
Engaged couples are called to live chastity in continence, keeping the gift for marriage (CCC 2350).
homily: Dear N. and N., dear families, in our tradition the betrothal is a solemn moment. It is not yet the sacrament of Matrimony; you are not yet husband and wife. But you are making a serious public promise, and the Church is glad to bless it.

The Church teaches that marriage is born from the free consent of a man and a woman (CCC 1625–1628). Free means without fear, without force and without pressure from anyone. Families have a precious role in helping their children choose well, but the choice belongs to the two persons who will make the vows. Today, in front of all of us, you show that this choice is yours.

The time between betrothal and marriage is a time of preparation. The Catechism says that the example and teaching of parents and families, and the preparation offered by the Church, help young people to understand the dignity of marriage (CCC 1632). Take part seriously in the marriage preparation course. Learn about the sacrament, about communication, about responsible parenthood according to the teaching of the Church, about forgiveness. A wedding lasts a day; a marriage lasts a lifetime.

The Church also asks engaged couples to live chastity in continence, keeping for marriage the gift that belongs to marriage (CCC 2350). This is not a rule against love; it is a school of love. It teaches respect, patience and self-control, which you will need every day of married life.

Finally, prepare spiritually. Make a good confession before the wedding. Pray together. Come to the {Q} together. Dear families, pray for them and be generous with your support. And dear N. and N., may this betrothal be the first step of a marriage that is truly Christian, faithful and open to life.

marriage.verse: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
points: A covenant, not a contract
Marriage is a covenant of the whole life, sealed before God; for the baptised it is a sacrament.
Christ and the Church
St Paul compares the love of husband and wife to the love of Christ for his Church: faithful, self-giving, to the cross.
One, faithful, for ever
“What God has joined together, let no one separate.” Unity, fidelity, openness to life.
Invite Jesus
At Cana the wine ran out. In every marriage it sometimes does. Keep Jesus and Mary at the table.
homily: Dear bride and bridegroom, dear families, today two lives become one. Jesus said: “They are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” What happens at this altar is not only a promise between you; it is God himself joining you.

Marriage is a covenant, not a contract. A contract says, “I will give as long as you give.” A covenant says, “I give myself, whatever comes.” St Paul tells husbands and wives to love as Christ loved the Church. And how did Christ love? To the cross.

At Cana the wine ran out in the middle of the wedding. In every marriage, at some time, the wine runs out: patience, money, health, feelings. Do what Mary said: “Do whatever he tells you.” Keep Jesus in your home. Pray together every day. Forgive before you sleep. Come together to the {Q}.
Dear families, support this new home with your prayers and your respect, not with interference. And may God, who began this good work in you today, bring it to completion. Amen.
marriage.prayer: Lord God, you have joined these two in holy marriage. Make their love faithful and fruitful, keep Jesus and Mary in their home, and when the wine runs short, fill their jars again. Amen.

opts.a: Cana: when the wine runs out
points: Jesus at a wedding
Jesus began His signs at a wedding (John 2:1–11). He cares about married life.
The wine ran out
Every marriage has days when joy runs short.
Do whatever He tells you
Mary's advice is the secret of a good marriage (John 2:5).
The best wine kept
Love purified by Christ grows better with time.
homily: Dear N. and N., the Gospel of Cana tells us that the first sign Jesus worked was at a wedding (John 2:1–11). He could have chosen a temple or a palace. He chose a village celebration. It tells us something: Jesus loves marriage, and He wants to be present in yours.

At Cana the wine ran out. It was an embarrassment for the young couple. Every marriage, sooner or later, has a day when the wine runs out: when feelings are tired, when money is short, when illness or children or in-laws bring tension. Do not be surprised when that day comes. It does not mean your marriage has failed. It means it is time to call Jesus.

Notice who noticed the problem first: Mary. She went to her Son and then said to the servants: do whatever He tells you (John 2:5). This is the best advice anyone can give you today. When you do not know what to do, ask Jesus, and do what He tells you in the Gospel and in the teaching of His Church. Pray the Rosary together; let Mary notice your needs before you do.

Jesus told the servants to fill the jars with water, ordinary water, up to the brim. Then it became wine. Your marriage is made of ordinary water: cooking, working, cleaning, patience, apologies. Fill those jars to the brim with love, and Christ will change them into wine.

The steward said: you have kept the good wine until now (John 2:10). That is God's promise for a Christian marriage. The best is not the wedding day; the best is later, when love has been tested and purified. Dear N. and N., may your best wine be served in your old age, and may everyone who visits your home taste the joy of Cana.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the sacrament of Matrimony
points: Made by God
Marriage is written in creation itself (Genesis 1:27–28; CCC 1603).
Raised to a sacrament
Christ made marriage between the baptised a sign of His love for the Church (Ephesians 5:25–32; CCC 1601, 1617).
Unity and indissolubility
A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power (Mark 10:9; CCC 1640, 1644).
Open to life
Marriage is ordered to the good of the spouses and to children (CCC 1652–1654).
homily: Dear N. and N., dear families and friends, today we celebrate a sacrament. It is good to recall what the Church believes about it, because a wedding is more than a beautiful ceremony.

Marriage was not invented by any culture or law. It was written by God into creation: male and female He created them, blessed them and told them to be fruitful (Genesis 1:27–28). The Catechism says that God Himself is the author of marriage (CCC 1603). Jesus pointed back to that beginning: the two become one flesh, and what God has joined together, no one must separate (Mark 10:6–9).

Christ raised marriage between baptised persons to the dignity of a sacrament (CCC 1601). St Paul says that the love of husband and wife is a sign of the love between Christ and His Church (Ephesians 5:25–32). That means your love is meant to show the world how Christ loves: faithfully, totally, to the point of sacrifice. In the Latin tradition the spouses themselves are the ministers who confer the sacrament on each other by their consent; in the Eastern Churches the priest's blessing belongs to the very form of the sacrament. In every rite, Christ binds you together.

The Church teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage is one and indissoluble (CCC 1640, 1644). This is not a burden laid on you; it is a protection. Love that keeps an exit door open is always afraid. Love that is for ever can rest.

Finally, marriage is ordered both to your good and to the gift of children (CCC 1652). Be open to the children God gives you and raise them in the faith. Pray together, forgive quickly, come to the {Q} and to confession, and remember that the grace of this sacrament stays with you every day. The God who joins you today will give you the strength to remain one.

ordination.sub: For an ordination or a new priest's first celebration
ordination.verse: You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.
points: Chosen, not self-made
A priest does not choose himself; Christ chooses and the Church calls through the bishop.
Taken from among the people
“Every high priest chosen from among mortals is put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf” (Hebrews 5:1). He remains one of us and is given for us.
In the person of Christ
At the altar and in the confessional, the priest acts in the person of Christ the Head. The gift is greater than the man.
The family and the parish
Thank the parents who gave a son; pray for vocations from this parish.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today is a day of great joy for this parish and this family. One of our own stands at the altar as a priest of Jesus Christ. Jesus says to him: “You did not choose me but I chose you.”

A priest is taken from among the people and given back to the people. He is not an angel; he is a son of this soil, with his own weaknesses. That is exactly why God's choice is so moving. Through his hands bread and wine will become the Body and Blood of Christ; through his words sins will be forgiven. The gift is far greater than the man.

Dear new priest, Jesus appointed you “to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” The fruit that lasts is not buildings or popularity; it is souls brought to God. Stay close to the Lord in prayer, love the poor, and never be ashamed to ask for forgiveness.
Dear parents, thank you for giving your son to God. Dear parish, pray for him every day, and pray that more of your sons and daughters will hear the call. Amen.
ordination.prayer: Lord Jesus, eternal High Priest, you have chosen this servant for your altar. Keep him holy, humble and joyful; make his priesthood bear fruit that will last, and raise up many more labourers for your harvest. Amen.

opts.a: Jeremiah: called before birth
points: Known before birth
Before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5): the call comes from God.
I am only a boy
Jeremiah's fear was real; God's answer was presence (Jeremiah 1:6–8).
Words in your mouth
The Lord touched his mouth (Jeremiah 1:9): a priest speaks God's word, not his own.
A hard and beautiful road
Jeremiah suffered for his mission; the priest too shares the cross.
homily: Dear Father N., dear family, dear brothers and sisters, today we listen to the call of the prophet Jeremiah. God tells him that before He formed him in the womb He knew him, and before he was born He consecrated him (Jeremiah 1:5). A vocation does not begin with our decision. It begins in the heart of God.

Jeremiah's first answer was fear: I do not know how to speak, for I am only a boy (Jeremiah 1:6). Every honest priest has felt this. The task is too big. People will expect wisdom, holiness, patience, energy. God does not answer Jeremiah by saying that he is strong enough. He answers: do not be afraid, for I am with you (Jeremiah 1:8). A priest does not rely on his talents, but on the presence of the One who sent him.

Then the Lord touched Jeremiah's mouth and said: I have put my words in your mouth (Jeremiah 1:9). Father, from today your words carry a weight that is not yours. You will say: this is my Body. You will say: I absolve you from your sins. These are the words of Christ in your mouth. Never let your own opinions crowd them out. Preach the Gospel, not yourself.

Jeremiah's life was not easy. He was mocked, imprisoned and misunderstood. Priesthood too is not a career; it is a share in the cross. There will be lonely evenings, criticism and fatigue. In those moments go back to the altar, to the tabernacle, to your breviary, to your confessor and to your brother priests.

Dear family, thank you for the gift of this son. Dear people, pray for him every day; a priest is carried by the prayers of his people. And dear Father N., may you celebrate this first {Q} with the same wonder with which you will celebrate your last. The God who knew you before you were born will not abandon you.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the ministerial priesthood
points: One priesthood of Christ
Christ is the one High Priest; the ministerial priesthood is a participation in His (Hebrews 5:1–10; CCC 1545).
In the person of Christ the Head
The ordained priest acts in persona Christi Capitis (CCC 1548).
Three tasks
To teach, to sanctify and to govern, in communion with the bishop (CCC 1592).
An indelible character
Holy Orders, like Baptism and Confirmation, is conferred once for all (CCC 1582).
homily: Dear Father N., dear family and friends, today we thank God for a new priest. It is a good moment to remember what the Church believes about the priesthood.

There is only one priest in the full sense: Jesus Christ. The Letter to the Hebrews says that every high priest is taken from among men and appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and that Christ did not glorify Himself but was called by the Father (Hebrews 5:1–5). He offered Himself once for all on the Cross. All the baptised share in His priesthood by offering their lives; the ordained priest shares in it in a different way, by sacramental ordination, for the service of the whole people (CCC 1545, 1547).

When the priest celebrates the sacraments, he acts in the person of Christ the Head (CCC 1548). It is Christ who baptises, Christ who forgives, Christ who offers the {Q}. This is why the Church can say that the sacraments are valid even when the minister is weak: their power does not come from his holiness but from Christ. And this is also why the priest must strive to be holy, so that his life does not contradict the words he speaks.

The priest receives a threefold mission: to teach the Word of God faithfully, to sanctify the people through the sacraments, and to guide the community as a shepherd, always in communion with his bishop (CCC 1592). He is not the owner of the parish but its servant.

Holy Orders marks the soul with an indelible character; it is received once for all (CCC 1582). Father, you will be a priest for ever. Dear people, love your priests, pray for them, correct them gently when needed, and encourage vocations in your families. And let us all ask the Lord of the harvest to send more labourers into His harvest.

profession.sub: For first or final vows of a religious brother or sister
profession.verse: The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot.
points: Everything for Christ
“Whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ” (Philippians 3:7).
Three vows
Poverty, chastity and obedience: not a loss of life, but a life given wholly to God.
A sign for all
Religious life reminds every Christian that God alone is enough and that heaven is our home.
Gratitude
Thank the family and the community; pray for perseverance.
homily: Dear sister (brother), today you give your whole life to God by the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. With the psalmist you say: “The Lord is my chosen portion and my cup.”

In the Gospel a rich young man came to Jesus and went away sad, because he could not let go. Today we see the opposite: someone who has heard “Come, follow me” and says yes. St Paul says, “I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.”

The vows are not chains. Poverty sets you free from possessions; chastity sets your heart free to love everyone; obedience sets you free from yourself. And your life becomes a sign for all of us that God alone is enough.
Dear family, you are not losing a daughter (son); you are giving her (him) to God, and God is never outdone in generosity. Let us pray that she (he) may be faithful to the end. Amen.
profession.prayer: Lord, you are the portion and the cup of your servant. Accept the offering of this life, keep her (him) faithful to the vows professed today, and make her (his) joy a witness to your love. Amen.

opts.a: Samuel: speak, Lord, your servant is listening
points: A voice in the night
The boy Samuel heard his name called in the temple (1 Samuel 3:1–10).
Help to recognise God
Eli helped Samuel to understand that it was the Lord.
A listening life
Religious life is a life of listening: prayer, obedience, community.
Here I am
Samuel's answer becomes the vow: here I am, for you called me.
homily: Dear Sister (Brother) N., today we hear the story of a boy who could not sleep. Samuel was lying in the temple at night when he heard his name. He ran to the old priest Eli, thinking Eli had called him. Three times this happened, until Eli understood that it was the Lord (1 Samuel 3:1–10).

A vocation often begins like that: a voice we do not fully understand, a restlessness, a desire we cannot explain. Many of us needed an Eli: a priest, a sister, a parent or a friend who helped us recognise that it was God calling. Today let us thank all the Elis in your life who helped you hear.

Eli taught Samuel a simple prayer: speak, Lord, for your servant is listening. That sentence is a summary of religious life. Your day will be shaped by listening: in prayer and the Liturgy of the Hours, in the Word of God, in obedience to your superiors, in the voices of the poor and the sick you serve. Obedience is not losing your freedom; it is choosing to listen to God through the community He has given you.

Samuel grew up, and the Lord was with him. He became a prophet for all Israel. Your consecration too is not for yourself. Your poverty reminds the world that God is enough. Your chastity shows that love can be total and undivided. Your obedience shows that true freedom is found in doing God's will.

Today, when you pronounce your vows, you are saying what Samuel said: here I am, for you called me. Say it again every morning. There will be days of dryness and days of joy, but the One who called you by name is faithful. Dear family, thank you for this gift. Dear community, receive her (him) with love. And may the Lord who called Samuel keep speaking to you all your life.

opts.a: Teaching homily: consecrated life in the Church
points: A special consecration
Rooted in Baptism, consecrated life is a closer following of Christ (CCC 916).
The evangelical counsels
Poverty, chastity and obedience, publicly professed (CCC 915).
A sign of the Kingdom
Consecrated persons point to the life of the world to come (CCC 933).
Many charisms, one Church
Monastic, apostolic, contemplative: all gifts of the Spirit for the Church (CCC 917–919).
homily: Dear Sister (Brother) N., dear family and community, today the Church receives the vows of one of her children. Let us recall what the Church teaches about this way of life.

Every Christian is consecrated in Baptism. Consecrated life is a deepening of that baptismal consecration: a way of following Christ more closely, under the action of the Holy Spirit, giving oneself totally to God loved above all (CCC 916). It is not a higher class of Christian, but a particular gift, given for the whole Church.

The heart of this life is the profession of the evangelical counsels: poverty, chastity and obedience (CCC 915). Jesus Himself lived poor, chaste and obedient to the Father. The rich young man in the Gospel was invited to sell all and follow Him, and went away sad (Mark 10:17–22). Today one of our own does not go away sad. She (he) follows.

The Catechism says that consecrated persons are a sign of the Kingdom: by their way of life they show that this world is passing and that God alone satisfies the human heart (CCC 933). In a world obsessed with having, pleasure and self-will, the three vows are a quiet and powerful witness.

The Spirit has given the Church many forms of consecrated life: hermits and monks, contemplative nuns, teaching and nursing congregations, missionaries (CCC 917–919). Each has its charism. Sister (Brother), love the charism of your founder, love your community and love the people you serve. Dear families, encourage vocations in your homes. And let us all offer this {Q} so that the one who makes her (his) vows today may be faithful until death.

sick.t: Anointing and Prayer for the Sick
sick.sub: For the anointing of the sick, or a Mass or prayer service for the sick
sick.verse: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
points: Not only for the dying
The anointing of the sick is for anyone seriously ill, before surgery, or weakened by old age (CCC 1514).
The Lord's own sacrament
“Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church and have them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:14).
Grace in suffering
Strength, peace and courage; forgiveness of sins; union with the Passion of Christ; healing of body if it is God's will.
The community cares
Visiting, bringing Communion, helping the family.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, especially you who are sick, Jesus says to you today: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.” You are not forgotten. You are at the centre of the Church's prayer.

Many people think the anointing of the sick is only for the dying, and so they call the priest too late. It is not so. St James says: “Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church.” This sacrament is for anyone seriously ill, before an operation, or weakened by age.

What does the sacrament give? Peace and courage; the forgiveness of sins; the grace to unite your suffering with the suffering of Christ; and, if it is God's will, healing of the body. Isaiah says of Jesus: “By his bruises we are healed.” Your pain, joined to his, is never wasted.
And to the families and the parish: the sick need our presence. Visit them, sit with them, bring them Holy Communion, help those who care for them. That too is the Church at prayer. Amen.
sick.prayer: Lord Jesus, you took our infirmities and bore our diseases. Look on your servants who are sick: give them strength and peace, forgive their sins, unite their suffering with your Passion, and, if it is your will, restore them to health. Amen.

opts.a: The paralysed man and his four friends
points: Carried by friends
Four men carried their friend to Jesus (Mark 2:1–12).
Through the roof
When the door was blocked, they made a way. Love finds a way.
Sins forgiven first
Jesus healed the soul before the body.
Get up and walk
Healing may be of body, mind or spirit, always according to God's will.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, especially those of you who are ill, today's Gospel tells of a man who could not walk to Jesus by himself. Four friends carried him on a mat. When they could not get through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof, opened it and lowered him down in front of Jesus (Mark 2:1–12).

Many of you who are sick feel like that man: unable to do the things you once did, dependent on others. Do not be ashamed. In this Gospel the paralysed man is not a burden; he is the centre of the story. Jesus looks at him first. And the faith of his friends matters: Jesus saw their faith. Your family, your caregivers and this parish are your four friends today, carrying you to the Lord in prayer.

Notice what Jesus says first: your sins are forgiven. The people expected a miracle of the body; Jesus began with the soul. Illness often brings fear, regret and questions about life and death. The sacrament of Anointing brings peace to the soul: it forgives sins, if the sick person cannot go to confession, and gives strength and trust in God.

Then Jesus told the man to get up and walk, and he did. Sometimes the Lord gives physical healing through this sacrament, if it is good for the person's salvation. Sometimes He gives a different healing: courage to bear the illness, peace in the family, reconciliation with God and with others, a holy death. Every anointing is a meeting with Jesus who heals.

To the families and caregivers: thank you. Your patience is a hidden prayer. To the parish: visit the sick, bring them Communion, do not forget them. And to you who are suffering: unite your pain with the Cross of Jesus. Offer it for the Church, for your family, for priests. Your suffering is not wasted; in Christ it becomes a gift.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the sacrament of Anointing
points: Instituted by Christ
Promulgated by St James: let him call the elders of the Church (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510).
Who may receive it
Any of the faithful in danger due to sickness or old age, and before serious surgery (CCC 1514–1515).
The effects
Union with Christ's Passion, strength, peace, forgiveness of sins, sometimes bodily healing (CCC 1520–1523).
Do not wait
It is not only for the last moments; call the priest early.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, many people still think that the Anointing of the Sick is only for the moment of death. When the priest is called, the family fears the worst. Today let us correct that idea with the teaching of the Church.

The Letter of St James says: is anyone among you sick? Let him call the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; the prayer of faith will save the sick, the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins he will be forgiven (James 5:14–15). The Church sees here a sacrament instituted by Christ and promulgated by the apostle (CCC 1510–1511).

Who may receive it? Any baptised person who begins to be in danger because of sickness or old age. It may be received before a serious operation, and repeated if the illness becomes worse or a new illness arises (CCC 1514–1515). So do not wait until the sick person is unconscious. Call the priest while the person can still pray, confess and receive Communion.

What does the sacrament do? It gives the grace of the Holy Spirit: strength, peace and courage to overcome the difficulties of illness. It unites the sick person to the Passion of Christ, so that suffering takes on a new meaning. It forgives sins, if the person was not able to confess. And sometimes, if it serves the salvation of the soul, it restores bodily health (CCC 1520–1523). For those near death, together with confession and Viaticum, it prepares for the passage to the Father.

The priest anoints the forehead and the hands with blessed oil, praying that the Lord in His love and mercy may help the sick person with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Families, do not be afraid of this sacrament. It is a gift of Christ's tenderness. Bring your sick to the Church, and bring the Church to your sick.

funeral.sub: For the funeral of a Christian
funeral.verse: I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live.
points: Grief is not faithless
Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus. Tears are allowed; despair is not.
Christ has conquered death
“I am the resurrection and the life.” Death is not the end but a passage.
We pray for the dead
The Church has always prayed and offered the Eucharist for the departed, that they may be purified and enter the joy of God (CCC 1032; 2 Maccabees 12:46).
Speak of the person truthfully
Remember the life with gratitude, without exaggeration; the focus is Christ's mercy.
homily: Dear family and friends, we have come together with heavy hearts to say farewell to our brother (sister) N. At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, Jesus wept. So we too may weep today. Christian faith does not forbid tears; it gives them hope.

To Martha, standing in her grief, Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live.” These are the words we hold on to today. For the believer, death is not a wall but a door. Christ has passed through it before us and has broken its power.

We remember N. with gratitude: for his (her) love, his (her) work, his (her) faith. But we do not canonise anyone at a funeral. We entrust him (her) to the mercy of God. From the earliest times the Church has prayed and offered the Eucharist for the dead, so that they may be purified and enter fully into God's joy. That is the greatest gift we can still give: our prayer.
Dear family, you are not alone. The parish stands with you. And one day, by God's mercy, we hope to meet again where every tear will be wiped away. Eternal rest grant unto him (her), O Lord. Amen.
funeral.prayer: Lord Jesus, resurrection and life, receive our brother (sister) N. into your mercy. Forgive his (her) sins, bring him (her) into the light of your face, and console all who mourn with the hope of the resurrection. Amen.

opts.a: Martha at the tomb: faith in tears
points: If you had been here
Martha's honest complaint to Jesus (John 11:21). Grief may speak freely to God.
I am the resurrection
Jesus answers grief with a person, not a theory (John 11:25).
Do you believe this?
The question is put to each of us at this coffin (John 11:26).
Jesus wept
God does not watch our sorrow from a distance (John 11:35).
homily: Dear family of N., dear friends, when Lazarus died, his sister Martha went out to meet Jesus and said: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (John 11:21). Perhaps some of you have said something similar in these days: Lord, where were you? Why now? Why like this? Martha teaches us that we may say such things to God. Faith is not pretending that we do not hurt.

Jesus did not give Martha a lecture. He gave her Himself: I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live (John 11:25). He did not say: there will be a resurrection one day. He said: I am. Our hope is not an idea; it is a person who has walked through death and come out on the other side.

Then Jesus asked Martha: do you believe this? (John 11:26). Today that question stands beside this coffin and is addressed to each of us. Do we believe that death is not the end? Do we believe that N., baptised into Christ, is called to share His risen life? Martha answered: yes, Lord, I believe. Let us make her answer ours, even if our voice trembles.

And a little later the Gospel says simply: Jesus wept (John 11:35). He knew that He was about to raise Lazarus, and still He wept. God is not indifferent to your tears. He stands with you at this grave. Christian hope does not cancel grief; it gives grief a horizon.

So let us do what the Church does: pray for N., that any stain of sin may be washed away and that he (she) may see the face of God. Let us offer this {Q} for him (her). Let us thank God for the good he (she) did. And let us live in such a way that one day we may all meet again in the house of the Father, where there will be no more tears.

opts.a: Teaching homily: what the Church believes about death
points: Death is real
Death is the end of earthly life and the separation of soul and body (CCC 997, 1007).
Judgement and mercy
At death each person receives eternal recompense in a particular judgement (CCC 1021–1022).
Purification
Those who die in God's friendship but still imperfectly purified undergo purification, called purgatory (CCC 1030–1031).
Our prayer helps
The Church offers the Eucharistic sacrifice and prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:46; CCC 1032).
homily: Dear family and friends of N., at a funeral we are confronted with the question every human being must face: what happens when we die? Let us listen to what the Church teaches, so that our grief may be held by faith.

Death is real. It is the end of our earthly pilgrimage and the separation of the soul from the body (CCC 997, 1007). The body we lay to rest today will return to the earth, and we treat it with reverence because it was a temple of the Holy Spirit. But the soul does not die. And at the end of time, God will raise our bodies, transformed and glorious, as He raised the body of Jesus (CCC 997–1001).

At the moment of death each person stands before Christ in the particular judgement (CCC 1022). This is not a cold courtroom. The Judge is the One who died for us. Yet the judgement is real: our life, our choices, our love or lack of love, will be seen in the light of truth.

Many of us die in God's friendship but not yet completely purified. The Church teaches that such souls undergo a purification, which she calls purgatory, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven (CCC 1030–1031). It is a work of mercy, the fire of God's love cleansing what is still selfish in us.

And here we can help. From the earliest times the Church has prayed for the dead; already Judas Maccabeus made an offering for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:43–46; CCC 1032). The greatest prayer we can offer is the {Q}. So let us not only mourn N.; let us pray for him (her), today and in the months ahead. Have {Q} offered on the anniversaries, give alms in his (her) name, and pray the Rosary for his (her) soul. Love does not end at the grave; it becomes prayer.

memorial.t: Commemoration of the Departed (41st day, anniversary)
memorial.sub: For the 41st-day remembrance, a death anniversary or a memorial Mass
memorial.verse: In my Father's house there are many dwelling places. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?
points: Love does not end
Death separates us for a time; it does not break the communion of saints.
Why we offer the Eucharist
The {Q} offered for the departed is the greatest help we can give them (CCC 1032, 1371).
Remember to imitate
Recall one virtue of the departed and ask the family to carry it on.
Our own preparation
Every remembrance is also a reminder: live today ready to meet the Lord.
homily: Dear family and friends, we have gathered again to remember N. The days have passed, the first tears have perhaps become quieter, but the love remains. And love, in Christ, does not end.

Jesus says: “In my Father's house there are many dwelling places.” Our dear ones have not disappeared; they have gone ahead. We believe in the communion of saints: those on earth, those being purified, and those in heaven form one family in Christ.

That is why we offer this {Q} for N. The Church teaches that the Eucharistic sacrifice is offered also for the faithful departed, that they may enter the light and peace of Christ. Our prayer is the most precious gift we can still give.

Let us also remember to imitate. Think of one good thing N. did, and continue it in your own life. And let each of us live today in such a way that we are ready to meet the Lord. Eternal rest grant unto him (her), O Lord. Amen.
memorial.prayer: Lord, in your Father's house there are many dwelling places. Grant N. a place of light and peace, and keep us faithful, so that one day we may all be gathered together in your kingdom. Amen.

opts.a: The many rooms of the Father's house
points: Do not let your hearts be troubled
Jesus speaks these words at the Last Supper, on the eve of His own death (John 14:1).
A place prepared
In the Father's house there are many dwelling places (John 14:2).
I will come again
Christ comes for each of us at death and at the end of time (John 14:3).
The way
Jesus Himself is the way to that house (John 14:6).
homily: Dear family, it is some time now since N. left us. The first shock has passed, but the absence remains. At the table, at festivals, in small daily things, we notice that someone is missing. Today we gather to pray for N. and to let the word of Jesus comfort us again.

At the Last Supper, on the night before He died, Jesus said to His disciples: do not let your hearts be troubled (John 14:1). He knew that they would soon be shattered by grief. He did not deny that sorrow would come; He gave them a promise to hold on to.

In my Father's house there are many dwelling places, He said; I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2). Think of what this means. Jesus speaks of heaven not as a cold idea, but as a home, a house with rooms, a family dwelling. We pray today that N. may be welcomed into that home, purified of every sin and filled with the joy of God.

Jesus added: I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also (John 14:3). The Christian does not die alone. Christ comes to meet each of His own. And when Thomas asked how they could know the way, Jesus answered: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

So the best way to honour N. is to walk that way ourselves. Let us remember the good he (she) taught us and live it. Let us forgive whatever needs forgiving. Let us keep praying for him (her), especially in the {Q}, and keep our own lamps ready. One day, God willing, the family that is divided today by death will be gathered again in the Father's house.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the communion of saints
points: One family in three states
Pilgrims on earth, souls being purified, saints in glory: one Church (CCC 954).
Exchange of spiritual goods
Our prayer can help the dead; their intercession can help us (CCC 958).
Why the Eucharist
The {Q} is the most powerful prayer for the departed (CCC 1371).
Remembering well
Anniversaries, alms, indulgences and a changed life.
homily: Dear family and friends, in the Creed we say every Sunday: I believe in the communion of saints. Today, as we remember N., let us look at what those words mean.

The Church teaches that there is one family of God in three conditions: some of us are still pilgrims on earth; others have died and are being purified; others are in glory, contemplating God (CCC 954). Death does not break this family. It changes the way we are together, but it does not end our bond.

Within this family there is an exchange of gifts. We can help those who are being purified by our prayers, our sacrifices and our good works; and those who are with God can intercede for us (CCC 958, 1032). That is why we do not only remember N. with photographs and stories. We pray for him (her).

The greatest of all prayers is the {Q}. In it the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, and the Church has always offered it for the living and the dead (CCC 1371). St Monica, dying far from home, asked her son Augustine only one thing: remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are. That is still the best gift we can give our dead.

How else can we remember well? By giving alms in their name, by seeking indulgences for them, by visiting their grave with prayer, and above all by living the faith they handed on to us. Dear family, may N. rest in the peace of Christ, and may we all one day share with him (her) the joy of the saints.

weddingjubilee.sub: For the silver, golden or any anniversary of marriage
weddingjubilee.verse: But you have kept the good wine until now.
points: The good wine kept until now
At Cana the best wine came last. Years of faithful love can become better, not weaker.
Grace, not only effort
A long marriage is a work of God's grace as much as of human effort.
Forgiveness as daily bread
“Bear with one another and… forgive each other” (Colossians 3:13).
A witness to the young
In a time of broken families, faithful couples preach without words.
homily: Dear N. and N., today we thank God with you for these years of married life. At Cana the steward said: “Everyone serves the good wine first… But you have kept the good wine until now.” Your jubilee is that good wine.

When you stood at the altar years ago, you could not know everything that was coming: children, joys, illnesses, debts, misunderstandings, reconciliations. But you kept your promise. That is not only your achievement; it is God's grace working in two ordinary hearts.

St Paul describes the secret: “Bear with one another and, if anyone has a complaint against another, forgive each other; just as the Lord has forgiven you.” Forgiveness was your daily bread. Teach that to your children and grandchildren.
In a time when many marriages break, your faithfulness is a sermon without words. May the Lord who kept the best wine until now give you many more years together. Amen.
weddingjubilee.prayer: Lord Jesus, guest at Cana, we thank you for the years of love you have given N. and N. Renew their love, bless their children and grandchildren, and keep the best wine for the years still to come. Amen.

opts.a: Tobit's blessing: growing old together
points: A prayer from the beginning
Tobias and Sarah asked to grow old together (Tobit 8:7). Today that prayer is answered.
Years of ordinary faithfulness
Most of a marriage is not dramatic, but daily.
Wounds and healing
Every long marriage has wounds that forgiveness has healed.
Blessing the next generation
Your fidelity is a blessing for your children and grandchildren.
homily: Dear N. and N., on the night of their wedding, Tobias and Sarah stood up and prayed. They asked God for mercy and that they might grow old together (Tobit 8:7). Today we see that prayer answered in you. You have grown older together, and you are still here, side by side.

When you married, you could not know what was coming. There were joys you never imagined: children, grandchildren, achievements, festivals. There were also sorrows: illnesses, deaths in the family, financial worries, misunderstandings. Most of all there were thousands of ordinary days: meals cooked, bills paid, children taken to school, prayers said at night. Holiness was hidden in those ordinary days.

No long marriage is without wounds. Somewhere along the road each of you has hurt the other, and each has had to forgive. That is not a failure of your marriage; it is its strength. A marriage lasts not because two perfect people met, but because two imperfect people kept choosing to forgive.

Today you are a sign for the whole parish, and especially for the young. Many young people are afraid of commitment because they see so many broken homes. Your faithfulness tells them: it is possible, with God's grace. Tell them your story. Tell them what helped you through hard times.

So we thank God with you. We pray for your health and peace in the years ahead. And we ask the Lord, who changed water into wine at Cana, to keep pouring His good wine into your home until the end. Renew today, with grateful hearts, the promises you made on your wedding day.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the grace of the sacrament
points: A permanent grace
The sacrament gives a grace that remains throughout married life (CCC 1641–1642).
Christ stays with the spouses
He dwells with them to help them rise after falls and forgive (CCC 1642).
A domestic church
The Christian family is a community of faith, hope and love (CCC 1655–1657).
Grace for old age
The same grace sustains spouses in illness and age.
homily: Dear N. and N., dear family, a wedding jubilee is a good moment to recall something the Church teaches that many couples forget: the sacrament of Matrimony is not only a ceremony on one day. It is a living grace that remains with the spouses every day of their lives.

The Catechism says that Christ dwells with the spouses, gives them the strength to take up their crosses and follow Him, to rise again after they have fallen, to forgive one another, to bear one another's burdens and to love one another with a supernatural, tender and fruitful love (CCC 1642). Every year of your marriage, Christ has been at work, often unnoticed.

When you forgave each other after a quarrel, that was grace. When you stayed beside each other in illness, that was grace. When you prayed together for a child in trouble, that was grace. Today we thank God not only for your effort, real as it is, but for His faithfulness in you.

The Church calls the Christian family a domestic church: the first place where faith is lived and handed on (CCC 1656). In your home your children learned to pray, to share, to forgive. Whatever they have become, they first saw faith in you. That is a priesthood of parents that only God can measure.

The grace that sustained your youth will sustain your old age. There may be harder days ahead: weakness, illness, the loss of one another one day. Do not be afraid. The same Christ who joined you will carry you. Let us offer this {Q} in thanksgiving, and may God bless you and all your family.

priestjubilee.sub: For the jubilee of a priest or a religious
priestjubilee.verse: What shall I return to the LORD for all his bounty to me?
points: Gratitude first
The psalmist answers his own question: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:13).
Treasure in clay jars
“We have this treasure in clay jars, so that it may be made clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God” (2 Corinthians 4:7).
“Do you love me?”
Peter's threefold question is the question of every jubilee: love renewed after years of service and failure.
Thank the people
A priest's or religious's life is woven with the people they served.
homily: Dear Father (Sister) N., dear friends, today we join the psalmist in asking: “What shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me?” And the psalm answers: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” For a priest that is exactly what happens every day at the altar.

St Paul says: “We have this treasure in clay jars.” After many years of service, a jubilarian knows better than anyone how fragile the jar is, and how great the treasure. The fruit of these years belongs to God.

By the lake, the risen Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” Peter had failed him, and yet Jesus entrusted his sheep to him again. Every jubilee is that question renewed: after all these years, do you love me? And the answer is: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”
Let us thank God for this life given, and let us pray that our families may give more sons and daughters to the service of the Lord. Amen.
priestjubilee.prayer: Lord, we thank you for the years of service of your servant N. Renew the grace of the first day, forgive what was lacking, and keep him (her) faithful in love until the end. Amen.

opts.a: Peter on the shore: a love that was restored
points: A charcoal fire
Peter denied Jesus beside a fire; Jesus restored him beside a fire (John 18:18; 21:9).
Three questions
Three denials, three declarations of love (John 21:15–17).
Feed my sheep
The priest's love for Christ is shown in care for the people.
Follow me
Even after many years, the call is the same (John 21:19).
homily: Dear Father N., dear friends, today's Gospel takes us to the shore of the lake after the Resurrection. Jesus has prepared a charcoal fire and some fish for His tired disciples (John 21:9). The last time Peter stood by a charcoal fire, he denied Jesus three times (John 18:18). Now Jesus gives him a new beginning beside a fire.

Three times Jesus asks: Simon, son of John, do you love me? (John 21:15–17). Three denials, three declarations of love. Jesus does not ask Peter about his abilities, his plans or even his mistakes. He asks only about love. Father, after these years of ministry, this is still the only question that matters: do you love Him?

No priest reaches a jubilee without his own failures and regrets. There were moments of tiredness, impatience, discouragement, perhaps sin. Peter's story tells you that the Lord does not dismiss His servants for their weakness. He restores them. Today you can lay all those years before Him and hear Him ask again: do you love me?

And each time Peter answered, Jesus gave him a task: feed my lambs, tend my sheep. The love of a priest for Christ is shown in his love for the people. Think of the children you baptised, the couples you married, the sinners you absolved, the sick you anointed, the dead you buried, the hundreds of {Q} you offered. All of that was love made concrete.

Then Jesus said: follow me (John 21:19). Even after a jubilee, that call is not over. Father, keep following Him, in strength or in weakness, wherever He leads. Dear people, thank God for your priest and keep praying for him. Ad multos annos!

opts.a: Teaching homily: the gift and mystery of the priesthood
points: A gift, not a possession
The priesthood belongs to Christ; the priest is its steward (1 Corinthians 4:1).
The Eucharist at the centre
The priesthood exists above all for the Eucharist (CCC 1566).
The ministry of mercy
Through the priest Christ forgives sins (John 20:22–23; CCC 1461).
Faithful to the end
Perseverance is itself a grace to be asked for.
homily: Dear Father N., dear brothers and sisters, a priestly jubilee is a moment of gratitude. It is also a good time to recall, with the Church, what the priesthood is.

St Paul says that we should be regarded as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries (1 Corinthians 4:1). A steward does not own the house; he manages it for its master. The priesthood is not a personal achievement or a social position. It is Christ's gift, entrusted to a man for the sake of the people.

At the heart of the priesthood is the Eucharist. The Catechism says that it is in the Eucharistic worship that the priest exercises his sacred office most fully (CCC 1566). Father, over these years you have offered the {Q} thousands of times. Each time, Christ made present His one sacrifice through your hands. No other work of your ministry is greater than that.

The second great gift is mercy. On Easter evening the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and gave them the power to forgive sins (John 20:22–23). Only God can count the burdens that have been lifted in your confessional (CCC 1461). Those are hidden fruits that will be revealed only in heaven.

Finally, perseverance is itself a grace. Many begin; to remain faithful for so many years is a gift of God to be thanked for. Father, we thank God for you, and we ask Him to keep you faithful until the end. Dear people, pray for priests, love them, and encourage young men in your families to hear the call.

parishfeast.sub: For the patronal feast (perunnal), the dedication anniversary or the jubilee of a parish or institution
read: Matthew 5:1–12 or the Gospel of the patron saint
parishfeast.verse: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD!”
points: Why we celebrate a saint
The patron is a friend and intercessor who points to Christ, not a substitute for him.
A family of faith
The parish is the family of families: “citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).
The real decoration
Lights, processions and fireworks pass; confession, charity and reconciliation remain. Keep a share of the feast for the poor.
Looking forward
A jubilee looks back with thanks and forward with mission: who is missing from our parish today?
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the psalmist says: “I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the Lord!” Today our parish is glad. We celebrate our patron (our jubilee), and the whole family of the parish has come home.

Why do we honour a saint? Not because the saint replaces Christ, but because the saint shows us Christ. Our patron walked the road we walk and reached the goal. He (she) is our friend in heaven, praying for this parish.

Our feast has lights, processions, music and food, and that is good. But the real decoration of a feast is a cleansed heart: a good Confession, a family reconciled, a poor neighbour remembered. Let a share of this feast reach those who cannot celebrate.

And let us look forward. Who is missing from our parish today? Whom can we invite back? May our patron intercede for us, so that this parish may be a living house of God for the generations to come. Amen.
parishfeast.prayer: Lord God, we thank you for our parish and for the faith handed down to us. Through the intercession of our patron, make us one family in Christ, generous to the poor and faithful to the end. Amen.

opts.a: A cloud of witnesses: running the race
points: Surrounded by witnesses
The saints watch over our race (Hebrews 12:1).
Laying aside every weight
A feast is a call to let go of what slows us down.
Eyes fixed on Jesus
The patron saint always points to Christ (Hebrews 12:2).
The next lap
Each generation hands the faith on to the next.
homily: Dear parishioners, today we celebrate the feast of our patron (our parish jubilee). The Letter to the Hebrews says that we are surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, and therefore we should lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus (Hebrews 12:1–2).

Imagine a stadium. The runners are on the track, and the stands are full of those who have already finished the race. Our patron saint is in those stands, and so are the parishioners who built this church, the catechists who taught our parents, the grandmothers who prayed the Rosary in these pews. They are cheering for us.

A feast is a time of celebration: processions, decorations, music and food. All of that is good. But the letter tells us what really matters: lay aside every weight. What slows down our parish? Quarrels between families, gossip, divisions, indifference to the poor, half-empty pews on ordinary Sundays. A real feast would be to lay aside one of those weights.

The saints never point to themselves. Our patron points to Jesus: looking to Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). If our celebration is only about our saint, our village or our pride, it has missed the point. Every true devotion to a saint ends at the altar, in the {Q}, in Christ.

Finally, a race is run in relays. Our ancestors handed the faith to us; we must hand it on. Let this feast renew our parish: our catechism classes, our youth, our care for the sick and the poor, our unity. May our patron intercede for us, so that one day we too may join that cloud of witnesses.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the parish and the saints
points: What a parish is
A stable community of the faithful within a diocese, entrusted to a pastor (CCC 2179).
The church building
A house of prayer where the Eucharist is celebrated and reserved (CCC 1181).
Why we honour saints
Their intercession and example; worship belongs to God alone (CCC 956–957, 2132).
A missionary community
A parish exists to bring Christ to everyone in its territory.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on our parish feast it is good to ask: what is a parish, and why do we honour saints?

The Catechism says that a parish is a definite community of the Christian faithful, established on a stable basis within a particular Church, whose pastoral care is entrusted to a pastor under the authority of the bishop (CCC 2179). It is the place where the faithful gather for the {Q}, where children are baptised and taught, where couples are married and the dead are commended to God. It is the ordinary home of our faith.

Our church building is not just a hall. It is a house of prayer where the Eucharist is celebrated and where Christ is present in the tabernacle (CCC 1181). That is why we keep silence in church, dress respectfully and genuflect or bow before the Blessed Sacrament.

Why do we honour our patron? Not because saints take the place of God; adoration belongs to God alone. We venerate the saints because God's grace shone in them; they are our models and our intercessors (CCC 956–957). Asking a saint to pray for us is like asking a friend to pray for us, except that this friend is already with God.

Finally, a parish is not a club for those who are already inside. It is a missionary community, responsible for everyone living within its borders: the lonely, the poor, those who have drifted away, people of other faiths who deserve our respect and kindness. On this feast, let us ask our patron to make our parish a family that prays, welcomes and goes out.

house.sub: For the blessing of a new house (house warming)
house.verse: …but as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.
points: Unless the Lord builds the house
“Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).
Salvation came to Zacchaeus' house
“Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9): Jesus enters, and the household changes.
A domestic church
The home is where faith is first learnt: the prayer corner, the family rosary or evening prayer, the Bible on the table.
An open door
Hospitality to the poor and to guests is a blessing on the house.
homily: Dear family, today we bless this new home. Many years of work and saving are in these walls. But the psalm reminds us: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” Today you invite the Lord to be the true builder.
