When Jesus entered the house of Zacchaeus, he said: “Today salvation has come to this house.” A house is blessed not only by holy water but by the presence of Christ. Let him enter every room: the kitchen, the bedroom, the study, and especially the place of family prayer.

Joshua stood before the people and said: “As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord.” Make that your family motto. Keep a prayer corner, pray together every evening, keep the Bible open, and let the children see their parents kneel.
And keep your door open to guests and to the poor. A house that welcomes is a house that God fills with blessing. Peace be to this house and to all who live in it. Amen.
house.prayer: Lord Jesus, as you entered the house of Zacchaeus, enter this home. Bless all who live here and all who visit, keep sickness, quarrels and every evil far from it, and make it a home of prayer, peace and welcome. Amen.

opts.a: The house of Martha and Mary
points: Jesus as a guest
Martha welcomed Jesus into her home (Luke 10:38).
Busy hands
Martha was distracted by much serving; homes can be too busy for God.
The better part
Mary sat at His feet and listened (Luke 10:39, 42).
Both together
A Christian home needs Martha's work and Mary's prayer.
homily: Dear family, today we bless your new home. The Gospel tells us of a house in Bethany where Jesus loved to visit. Martha welcomed Him into her home (Luke 10:38). What a beautiful thing to say about a house: Jesus was welcome there.

Martha was busy with much serving. She was cooking and cleaning and worrying about getting everything right. There is nothing wrong with work; homes need it. But she became anxious and distracted, and even complained to Jesus about her sister (Luke 10:40). Many homes today are like that: full of activity, phones, television and tension, and too busy for God.

Mary sat at the feet of Jesus and listened. Jesus said that she had chosen the better part, which would not be taken from her (Luke 10:42). The better part is time with Him: a family prayer in the evening, the Bible on the table, a picture of the Sacred Heart or the Holy Family before which you gather.

A Christian home needs both Martha and Mary. It needs hands that serve: parents who work, children who help, meals shared together. And it needs hearts that listen: prayer together, forgiveness before sleep, Sunday {Q} as a family. When work and prayer are together, a house becomes a home, and a home becomes a domestic church.

So as I bless these walls, I bless more than a building. I pray that Jesus may always be welcome here; that this door may open to guests and to the poor; that this table may be a place of peace; and that everyone who lives here may one day be welcomed into the house of the Father.

opts.a: Teaching homily: sacramentals and the domestic church
points: What a blessing is
A sacramental by which the Church asks God's protection for persons and places (CCC 1667–1671).
Holy water and the cross
Signs that recall Baptism and the victory of Christ.
The domestic church
The family is the first school of prayer and virtue (CCC 1657, 2685).
Practical customs
Family prayer corner, enthronement of the Sacred Heart, grace before meals.
homily: Dear family, today's blessing is what the Church calls a sacramental. Let us understand what this means, so that this day bears fruit in your home.

Sacramentals are sacred signs instituted by the Church. They do not give grace in the way the sacraments do, but through the prayer of the Church they prepare us to receive grace and sanctify different circumstances of life (CCC 1667–1670). Among them, blessings come first: the Church praises God and asks His protection for persons, places and things (CCC 1671).

When I sprinkle holy water in your rooms, it recalls your Baptism, when you were washed and made children of God. When we place the cross on your wall, it proclaims that Christ, not fear or bad luck, rules this house. No evil eye, no superstition and no fear has power over a home that belongs to Christ. So you do not need charms or omens; you need faith, prayer and the sacraments.

The Catechism calls the Christian family a domestic church, the first place where children learn to pray and to live the virtues (CCC 1657, 2685). Your home is meant to be a little church: where the faith is believed, prayed and lived every day.

Some practical suggestions: keep a prayer corner with the cross, an image of Our Lady and the Bible. Pray together in the evening, even briefly. Say grace before meals. Consider the enthronement of the Sacred Heart. Bless your children before they go out. And come together to the {Q} every Sunday. Then this blessing will not end today; it will continue every day in your home.

school.t: Beginning of the School or Academic Year
school.sub: For a school Mass, the start of the academic year, or before examinations
school.verse: And Jesus increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor.
points: Ask for wisdom, like Solomon
Solomon asked not for riches but for “an understanding mind” (1 Kings 3:9).
Jesus grew
“Jesus increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor” (Luke 2:52): grow in all three.
Think about what is good
“Whatever is true, whatever is honorable… think about these things” (Philippians 4:8).
Teachers and parents
Thank teachers; parents are the first teachers.
homily: Dear children, dear teachers, a new year of learning begins. When God asked young King Solomon what he wanted, Solomon did not ask for riches or for victory over his enemies. He asked for wisdom, “an understanding mind”. God was so pleased that he gave him that and much more.

St Luke tells us that the boy Jesus “increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor.” Notice the three things: wisdom, which is learning; years, which is growing up; and favour with God and people, which is goodness. A good student grows in all three.

St Paul gives a simple rule for the mind: “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure… think about these things.” What you watch and read and think shapes who you become.
Let us thank God for our teachers and our parents, and let us begin this year asking, like Solomon, for wisdom. Amen.
school.prayer: Lord Jesus, you grew in wisdom and in favour with God and people. Bless our students, teachers and parents this year; give us understanding minds, honest work and kind hearts. Amen.

opts.a: Daniel and his friends: faithful in a foreign school
points: Chosen for study
Daniel and his friends were trained in the language and learning of Babylon (Daniel 1:3–5).
Faithful in small things
They kept their faith in a test about food (Daniel 1:8–16).
God gave knowledge
God gave them knowledge and skill in every aspect of learning (Daniel 1:17).
Ten times better
Faith and learning go together (Daniel 1:20).
homily: Dear students, teachers and parents, at the start of this school year let me tell you about four young students in the Bible: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. They were taken from Jerusalem to Babylon, the capital of a great empire, and chosen to study at the king's college for three years (Daniel 1:3–5).

It was a new place, new language and new friends, a bit like a new school or a new class. And there was pressure to become just like everyone else. The very first test was about food: the young men decided not to defile themselves with the king's rich food and wine, because of their faith. They asked politely for a ten-day trial, and at the end they were healthier than all the others (Daniel 1:8–16).

Here is the lesson: faithfulness often begins with small choices. Not copying in an exam. Not joining in when others bully someone. Not using bad language because everyone does. Praying before you study. Small choices make strong characters.

The Bible says that God gave these four young men knowledge and skill in every aspect of literature and wisdom (Daniel 1:17). When the king examined them, he found them ten times better than all the others (Daniel 1:20). Faith does not make you less intelligent; it makes you wiser. Study hard, and offer your study to God.

Teachers, you are shaping minds and hearts; thank you for your patience. Parents, encourage your children without crushing them. And students, begin every day this year with a short prayer: Lord, give me wisdom, help me to learn, and make me good. May this be a year of growth for all of you, in wisdom and in grace.

opts.a: Teaching homily: faith and reason
points: Two wings
Faith and reason are like two wings by which the human spirit rises to the truth (Fides et Ratio, introduction).
No real conflict
Truth cannot contradict truth (CCC 159).
Study as a vocation
Learning is a way of serving God and neighbour.
The virtues of a student
Diligence, honesty, humility and gratitude.
homily: Dear students, teachers and parents, as we begin a new academic year we ask God's blessing on our studies. It is a good moment to remember how the Church sees learning.

St John Paul II began his encyclical on faith and reason with a beautiful image: faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth (Fides et Ratio). A bird with one wing cannot fly. A faith that refuses to think becomes superstition; a reason that refuses God becomes arrogant and loses its way.

The Catechism teaches that there can never be a real conflict between faith and science, because the same God who reveals the mysteries of faith also gave us the light of reason; truth cannot contradict truth (CCC 159). Many great scientists were believers, and Catholic universities and schools have served the world for centuries. So study physics, history, mathematics and literature with an open mind and a believing heart.

Study is also a vocation. The young Jesus sat among the teachers in the Temple, listening and asking questions, and He grew in wisdom (Luke 2:46, 52). You are not studying only to get a job or to satisfy your parents. You are developing the gifts God gave you so that one day you can serve others.

Let me suggest four virtues for this year: diligence, to work steadily and not only before exams; honesty, never to cheat; humility, to ask for help and to help others; and gratitude, to thank your teachers and parents. Teachers, may you be patient witnesses of truth. Parents, support without pressure. And may the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of wisdom, guide us all this year.
